title: The Reynolds brothers' Sunday string group
summary: At about eleven he joins Bob and Harry Reynolds' Sunday sessions on Britannia Street. He lists the group: violinists Hilton Harrison and Rex, Bernie Shields on banjo, Charlie Hardy on ukulele and Bill Gibbons.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: Then along the line here, I would say around, I must have been no older than 12, maybe 11. We suddenly discovered there were other boys that were playing. We never had gotten together. Everybody was afraid to come out, afraid to show how little they knew. But finally, I went at an invitation to Bob and Harry Reynolds. They lived on Britannia Street, the corner of Marengo on the Uptown Woods Corner. And they asked me to bring my guitar. Well, I hid it in the bushes, and then I went on in and I listened to the two brothers, a guitar and mandolin. And I listened to them play, and I said to myself, they're not a damn bit better than I am. So then I went out and got my guitar and brought it out of the bushes and brought it in. Well then gradually, every Sunday, we'd meet over at their house about 1 o'clock, and we'd play straight through. We'd all get down to our BVDs, as hot as the hinges. And all of us stuck in this one upstairs bedroom. It was a big two-story house. Then around 5.30 in the evening, Mrs. Reynolds and Mr. Reynolds would have us all down to supper. And I remember it was the first time I'd ever heard Grace sit at meals. And there was a big tall, high muck-a-muck in the Methodist face. And he had whiskers, and he looked just like a bishop himself. But anyway, they put up with our music. In spite of it being jazz, in spite of his being very holy, none of us were drinking at the time. You see, we were kids there then, and they were encouraging it. Well, it finally wound up we had two guitars, a mandolin, a banjo, two violins, and no bass fiddle. And if I can run over in the names a little bit, it'll help me. I forgot a ukulele. There was Midget Harrison, Hilton Harrison, who was a classic violinist, and who gave recitals. His mother was a classic teacher. And boy, I have heard Joe Venuti, and I've heard the records of Eddie South, and what's the name of this? The Feli in France? Grappoli, Stephen Grappoli. And of course my enthusiasm to them, both as being a partner and marking a milestone, maybe I'm warped in his favor, but that guy could really tear a fiddle to pieces. Then we had a second violinist who was also a classic violinist, but who played an entirely different style, and he was a good foil for the other one. His name was Roland Rorschach. We called him Rex. He was a Spanish fellow, very Mexican-looking. And then Bernie Shields played a banjo, sometimes a mandolin. Then Bob and Harry Reynolds, and Harry was the mandolin, Bob the guitar. I was another guitar. And then Charlie Hardy came in with the ukulele. And then we had others that joined us at odd intervals. There was Bill Gibbons who played a guitar mandolin. It's the only one I've ever seen like it. It was a guitar about the size of a ukulele. But it had six double strings, you see, but it had a not too unpleasant tone, but it didn't add anything to the group, you see. No. Because he didn't play cording, he actually picked a melody on the thing.
